                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

  LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                              PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
  STANDARDS                  §                                       OF TEXAS
                             §

 GOOGLE, LANCIUM JOINT, AND TOTAL COMMENTS AND REDLINES FOR THE
                   PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

Introduction:
Google LLC, Lancium LLC, and TotalEnergies Renewables USA (together, the “Joint
Commenters”) appreciate the Commission’s efforts to implement PURA § 37.0561 and
ERCOT’s reintroduction of the batch process. The current framework reflects several
meaningful improvements, including:

   ●​ clearer gating criteria for entry into the batch and eligibility for energization;
   ●​ the absence of a major restudy during the batch refinement phase; and
   ●​ a more explicit linkage between the large load batch process and the Regional Planning
      Group (RPG) process.

Joint Commenters believe Project No 58481 and the batch study process must be evaluated
concurrently due to their inherently intertwined design and implementation. Accordingly, the
comments in this filing focus on aligning intermediate and final agreement criteria with the
timing, project maturity, and cost causation principles embedded in the batch framework.




                                                                                                       ​
      Figure 1: Suggestions for studies and financial obligations as it relates to the Batch Process


                                                    1
 Joint Commenters suggest the following changes (also shown in the pink box in Figure 1
above):

   1.​ Require the TSP to conduct a facilities study prior to the batch process and
       include it as a criteria for the intermediate agreement.
           -​ This assessment would establish technical feasibility and provide a preliminary
              estimate of customer-specific interconnection costs, allowing CIAC obligations
              and subsequent financial commitments to be grounded in project-specific data
              rather than assumptions. Requiring the facilities study as a precursor to the batch
              process will help reduce speculative projects. ​


   2.​ The financial security posted for the intermediate agreement should be fully
       refundable.
           -​ The intermediate agreement is executed prior to any transmission system
              planning studies. At this point in the process, there is zero line of sight to
              energization for a large load. In the draft Proposal for Publication, only 20% of the
              $50,000/MW financial security is refundable. It is unreasonable to require 80% of
              the security to be non-refundable before there is any assurance of energization.

          -​   In addition, retaining 80% of remaining funds after cost recovery is inconsistent
               with cost causation principles and operates as a penalty rather than a cost
               recovery mechanism.

          -​   Joint Commenters have maintained a defined “Security Threshold” at
               $50,000/MW financial security value in the attached redlines. However, Joint
               Commenters encourage the Commission to consider what an appropriate
               financial security threshold should be given expected costs.

          -​   Joint Commenters note the process creates significant timing pressures to
               negotiate a fully executed agreement during the 30 day commitment period. The
               Commission could simplify the process by making the intermediate agreement a
               standard form attachment to a full interconnection agreement, negotiated on the
               front end prior to batch submission, that defines the financial commitments and
               makes clear the exit provisions and refundability of securities throughout the
               batch process. This would allow for standardization of planning requirements and
               criteria across the system for batch purposes while still allowing for individual
               TSP contractual customization. ​


   3.​ A preliminary steady state study should be provided within 30 days from the start
       of the steady state analysis. After that, $6.5M of the financial security should
       become non-refundable to continue in the batch process.


                                                2
            -​   ERCOT and the TSPs should conduct a quick steady state model run to give an
                initial look at the capacity available on the base case model. This could be
                provided to large load customers as an initial screen for project viability. If large
                loads are interested in continuing at this stage, a nominal $6.5M in financial
                security is required to continue in the batch process. That is the amount Oncor
                stated is the typical estimated materials and supplies cost for a large load
                transmission interconnection.1
           -​   Joint Commenters have suggested a 14-day period for the large load customer to
                decide to remain in the batch process and a 30-day period to sign the
                interconnection agreement. The Commission should require the use of a
                standard interconnection agreement that allows refundability and exit after the
                first steady state study. ​

    4.​ Following the completion of the batch process final report, the large load
        customer should execute the interconnection agreement and pay the
        contribution-in-aid-of-construction (CIAC) or provide similar non-refundable
        financial obligations.
            -​ The interconnection agreement should securitize the load through minimum
               transmission charges for which the load must pay irrespective of slow load ramp
               or if it fails to materialize.
            -​ Section (f) (10) Financial Security for System Upgrades should be removed. The
               financial security provided with the intermediate agreement is effectively a
               financial security for system upgrades. Requiring additional financial security for
               system upgrades at the interconnection agreement stage may be duplicative.
               Once the project energizes, the transmission provider will begin collecting
               transmission charges from the customer, while the intermediate agreement
               financial security is released over the first five years. Maintaining separate
               upgrade security during this same period results in overlapping financial
               protections for the same transmission investment.
            -​ Section (f) (7) Non-refundable Interconnection Fees should be removed as it is
               inconsistent with cost causation principles. Assigning a disproportionate share of
               network-related costs to individual large loads, irrespective of broader system
               benefits, risks distorting investment signals and discouraging economic
               development.
            -​ Any financial security posted as part of the intermediate agreement should be
               released to the large load customer upon the posting of CIAC or other

                non-refundable security. Failure to refund securities while also charging CIAC is a
               double charge.​

    5.​ Following energization, the large load will pay a minimum transmission charge for
        at least five years.
            -​ Joint Commenters believe that a minimum transmission cost allocation charge
               structure, tied to actual service and long-term load commitments, is the best
               mechanism to ensure costs are fairly allocated in line with cost causation
               principles while supporting continued infrastructure investment.
            -​ To ensure that large load customers contribute equitably to transmission system
               costs, the Commission should establish a minimum transmission charge. This
               recommendation is consistent with frameworks already approved or being
               developed in multiple jurisdictions—including Arizona, Utah, West Virginia,
               Minnesota (Pending), Georgia, and Kansas2. To provide essential grid stability
               and secure long-term investment, this rate should be maintained for at least the
               first five years of operation, establishing a predictable cost-assignment
               foundation as these loads integrate into the system.

Joint Commenters suggest the following additional changes to the Proposal for Publication:

    1.​ At a minimum, Batch Zero should include projects that have already signed an
        agreement with the utility and have satisfied all CIAC and security payment obligations
        prior to July 15, 2026.
    2.​ Disclosure related to power supply and controllable load should be removed. No
        allocation for capacity should be considered in the planning study for Controllable Load
        Resources (CLRs) that have not been validated by the ERCOT process. CLR
        designation should be considered a pathway to expedite energization of
        already-approved loads but not as a pathway to grid capacity allocation when
        controllability has not been substantiated. ​

 The rulemaking should be timed so that policy decisions in the rule are able to inform the final
ERCOT Board vote. Overlapping dependencies create uncertainty, so the Commission should
create a clearly established plan to harmonize the ERCOT planning guide reforms and the
Substantive Rules in order to minimize uncertainty for all parties.

Conclusion:
These comments reflect Joint Commenters’ initial thoughts on how the draft Proposal for
Publication (PFP) could work together with the batch process introduced by ERCOT. Given that
ERCOT’s large load and batch study processes are still evolving, Joint Commenters offer these
additional refinements of the PFP to avoid misalignment between Commission rules, study
frameworks, and real-world project development timelines.

We look forward to continued engagement with the Commission and Staff to ensure the final
rule supports reliability, protects ratepayers, and allows credible, financeable large load projects
to move forward in a predictable and transparent manner.



Respectfully submitted,

 Christopher Matos                                   Evan Neel
 Energy Market Development Lead                      Sr. Director, Regulatory and Power Services
 Google LLC                                          Lancium LLC


 Greg Nelson
 Chief Development Officer

§25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.


      (a)   ​ Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an

      electric utility, a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large

      load customer to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a

      municipally owned utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service

      requirements for large load customers on their systems in addition to the standards

      adopted under this section. Any projects that have executed a signed agreement with

      the TSP prior to the effective date of this rule and have satisfied all CIAC and financial

      security payment obligations in accordance with the timelines specified in that

      agreement by the effective date of this rule shall be exempt from additional costs or

      financial security required by the following standards.




      (b) ​ Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:


              (1) ​ a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);


              (2) ​ an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first

              time; and


              (3) ​ an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.




      (c)   ​ Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the

      following meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:



                                                6
 (1) ​ Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage

facilities that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in

parallel with the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT

system.


(2) ​ Competitively      sensitive    information    --   Competitively   sensitive

information includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property

boundaries; commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development

prioritization; proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment

strategies; and financing structures as it relates to financial viability for

creditworthiness.   Competitively sensitive information does not include the

identity of a large load customer; general site location, such as load zone;

requested or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an

interconnection request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated

entities.


(3) ​ Contracted peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that

a   large   load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an

interconnecting TSP serve at a site as stated in the interconnection agreement.


(4) ​ Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric

utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to

provide retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large load

customer seeks to interconnect.


(5) ​ Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric

utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates

       (6) ​ Interconnection agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large

       load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting

       DSP, the interconnecting TSP after completion of the interconnection study and

       that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection (f) of this section.


       (7) ​ Interconnection study -- The set of studies that are required by ERCOT

       before a large load customer may be interconnected.


       (8) ​ Intermediate agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large

       load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting

       DSP, the interconnecting TSP before the interconnection study are initiated and

       that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection (d) of this section.


       (9) ​ Large load customer -- An entity requesting a new or expanded

       interconnection where the customer’s total expected non-coincident peak

       demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 MW.


       (10) ​ Requested peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that

       a large load customer requests, prior to executing an interconnection agreement,

       that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve at a site.


       (11) Financial Security threshold -- The maximum financial security required

       through the interconnection process shall not exceed $50,000/MW.


(d) ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Standards. ERCOT shall establish a process

consistent with this section.

       administrative protocols which create clear communication between the large

(d) ​ Intermediate agreement.          Before a large load interconnection request is

submitted to ERCOT for study, the large load customer must execute an intermediate

agreement with the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,

the interconnecting TSP. If the interconnecting DSP and the interconnecting TSP are

different entities, the intermediate agreement must specifically identify each entity’s

responsibilities under this section, including which entity will accept the study fee and

financial security from the large load customer. The intermediate agreement must meet

the requirements of this subsection.

       lease one or more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the

       customer’s planned facilities at the proposed location.

must disclose to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the

customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request for electric

service, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing,

delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request. A material change or delay

includes a delay of one or more years to the project’s projected date to realize its

requested or contracted peak demand, a 20% or greater change in the requested

or contracted peak demand, or a change in the location for the point of

interconnection.

(3) ​ Site-related studies and engineering services. A large load customer

must submit to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP the large load

the interconnecting TSP when requested, but no more frequently than quarterly.

must be accompanied by an attestation by an officer or official with binding

the submission is complete and accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A

large load customer must provide updates or progress reports to the

(5) ​ Schedule for phased energization of contracted peak demand. A

large load customer must disclose to the interconnecting DSP or the

interconnecting TSP the expected load ramp schedule, including the quarter and

year, for phased energization of the contracted peak demand expressed in MW,

power factor (PF), and megavolt-ampere reactive (MVAr) units.


(6) ​ Backup generating facilities. A large load customer must disclose to

the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the customer plans

to have on-site backup generating facilities. If the large load customer plans to

have on-site backup generating facilities, the large load customer must also

disclose the percentage of load it expects to cover with the backup generation,

       (C) ​ the fuel source and operational characteristics of each of the

       fuel storage limitations under the existing environmental permits; and


       (D) ​ how quickly each of the backup generating facilities can reach

       their full capacity to serve the load.
